exp.0:0:
This verse is the introduction to the book. It says that what follows is the word of the Lord, that is, a message that comes from God and not from the prophet himself. Zephaniah receives that word, and his ancestors are named back four generations. The explanation's note that an old spelling stands for a modern one, and that a certain marker equals a simple word, is left out, since neither appears in this verse. The message is placed in the days of King Josiah of Judah.

Zephaniah speaks on God's behalf to the kingdom of Judah. Josiah reigned after two very wicked kings, Manasseh and Amon, and later pushed forward religious reforms. Some think the list of ancestors, which reaches back to Hezekiah, might suggest that Zephaniah came from a royal family, but the Bible does not state this clearly. The message that follows is a serious warning of judgment because of idolatry and injustice.

God speaks within real history, with names and dates, and his word deserves to be taken seriously. Today we can read the Bible with humility, not choosing only what is comfortable, and ask God to correct us and draw us closer to him.
exp.0:2:
God announces a very wide-ranging judgment. He says he will take away men and animals, birds and fish, and also the stumbling blocks along with the wicked. That phrase is hard: it may refer to idols that caused people to fall, or to the obstacles that go with wicked people.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, in the time of King Josiah. The people of Judah practiced idolatry and mixed the worship of the LORD with the worship of Baal and the stars, as the following verse shows. The language recalls creation and the flood, and shows that human sin affects all of creation. Many believe this is very strong language of judgment, not necessarily a literal total destruction.

For today: examine whether there is something in your life that takes the place that belongs to God alone, and bring it to Him with sincerity. His judgment is serious, but He always first invites repentance.
exp.0:6:
Be silent before the Lord God, the explanation says, because his day of judgment is very near. "Prepared" means made ready, and "guests" are the people invited. God presents the judgment as a sacrifice already made ready, with guests set apart to take part.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks, sent by God to Judah. The people were mixing the worship of the Lord with the worship of the stars, and they had turned away from him. Interpreters differ about who the "guests" are: many think they are nations that God would use as instruments of judgment, such as Babylon.

For today: before we speak, make excuses, or shape our faith to suit our convenience, we can keep silence before God. There we examine sincerely whether we seek him truly or only in words, and we return to him in time.
exp.0:7:
It says that, when the "day of the Lord's sacrifice" comes, God will call to account the princes, the king's children, and those who are clothed with strange apparel. The phrase about punishing refers to coming to judge or to bring punishment. Being clothed with strange apparel most likely points to adopting the customs and religions of other peoples, though some also understand it as a sign of pride or luxury.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, in the time of the kingdom of Judah. He had already said that the Lord has prepared a sacrifice and its guests: it is an image of judgment. The leaders were meant to set the example, but they turned away from God and mixed themselves with other beliefs.

For today: examine what influences shape your faith and your decisions. If you have any leadership, in the family or in the church, remember that God expects faithfulness and a good example from you.
exp.0:9:
It says that when the day of God's judgment comes, cries of pain will be heard in different parts of Jerusalem. The first gate named was an entrance to the city, probably near the fish market. The second area seems to be another district of the city, and the hills are the high ground around it. The word for ruin refers to destruction. The howling is a loud cry of anguish.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He announces judgment because the leaders and the people were living in injustice, theft, deceit and indifference toward Him. Scholars understand the exact details of each place in different ways, but the message is clear: no one will escape the sight of God.

For today: do not live as if God did not care what you do. Examine your work, your money and your decisions honestly, and ask Him to help you live with integrity and return to Him with humility.
exp.0:12:
This verse says that the people's wealth will be taken as plunder and their houses will lie in ruins. Those who build houses will not live in them, and those who plant vineyards will not drink their wine.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He addresses those who lived at ease, trusting in their money, and who thought that God would do neither good nor harm. The image of people who sit comfortably and do not stir themselves, like wine left to settle without being disturbed, describes people who are indifferent and self-satisfied. This judgment announces the consequences of that spiritual carelessness.

For today: let us not place our security in what we have, nor live as if God were not involved in our lives. Let us examine honestly what we trust in, and seek God with humility each day.
exp.0:15:
This verse says that God's day of judgment will come with the sound of a trumpet, which in the Bible often signals war or danger, and with battle cries. That day will fall even on the fortified cities and the high towers, which people believed were safe.

Zephaniah was a prophet in Judah, probably in the time of King Josiah. God speaks to a people who had turned away from Him, and the prophet warns them of the judgment coming because of their sin. Scholars believe it refers to an invasion that was near, and also to God's final judgment. Some see both.

For today: do not place your security in what seems strong, such as money, position, or plans. Trust in God, and if He points out something in your life, return to Him with humility now.
exp.0:16:
God announces that he will bring distress upon the people, and they will walk like blind men, unsure what to do or where to go. The reason is clear: they have sinned against the Lord. The word "distress" here means causing suffering. The images of blood poured out like dust and flesh like dung show that their lives will be treated as worthless.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, who warns Judah and Jerusalem about the coming day of the Lord before their judgment. The verses before describe that day as dark and full of anguish. The next verse says that neither silver nor gold will be able to save anyone. Sin, above all turning away from God, has serious consequences.

Today we can take God seriously and not trust in money or in our own strength. If there is anything we have put above him, let us return to God with humility, for his mercy remains open to those who repent.
exp.1:5:
The explanation says that the coastal region, where the Philistine cities once stood, will be turned into pasture land. There will be simple shelters where shepherds live, who look after the flocks, and pens where the sheep are kept. The phrase about the coast refers to the strip of land along the Mediterranean Sea.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. He announces judgment on the Philistine cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron), which were hostile neighbors of Judah. The word for the people linked to the Philistines is usually understood as a people connected with them, although this is not known with complete certainty. Those cities, once full of people, would be left empty. The next verse promises that the rest of Judah would possess that land.

For today: God has the final word over powers that seem secure. We can trust that he cares for his people and that he can turn places of threat into places of rest.
exp.1:8:
God himself swears, by his own life, that Moab and Ammon will be destroyed just as Sodom and Gomorrah were. They will become a place overgrown with thorns and stinging weeds, a salt-ravaged wasteland where nothing grows, and a ruin for all time. The survivors of his people, meaning the faithful remnant of Israel, will take their possessions and inherit their land.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Moab and Ammon, neighbors of Israel, mocked God's people and grew proud by invading their territory. God says he has heard those insults and that their arrogance will have consequences.

For today: God sees the mockery and abuse directed at his people. You can entrust your grievances to him, without taking revenge, and remember that he opposes pride and cares for the humble.
exp.2:2:
The explanation says that Jerusalem's rulers, instead of caring for the people, attack them like roaring lions hunting their prey. The judges are like evening wolves: they arrive hungry and devour everything, leaving not even a bone for the morning. In other words, they take advantage of the people until they leave them with nothing.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks, delivering God's message, in the time before Judah's exile. The city, which almost everyone understands to be Jerusalem, did not listen to God or accept correction. The leaders, who were supposed to protect and do justice, became oppressors. Then God shows himself just, in the face of a city that no longer feels any shame.

For today: if you have any authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, use it to serve and not to gain advantage. And if something is not fair, remember that God sees and that he does care.
exp.2:4:
He says that God, who is just, lives in the midst of Jerusalem and never does wrong. Every morning he makes his justice clear, and he does not fail a single day. But the wicked person, the one who does evil, feels no shame.

Sofonías, a prophet of God, speaks to Judah and Jerusalem. He has just described their leaders: corrupt princes, judges, prophets, and priests. Against that wickedness, the prophet reminds them that God is different: he is faithful and just. The verses that follow show that God had already corrected other nations, but his people would not learn.

For today: God does not grow weary of being just or of calling us to change. If we sense that something in us is wrong, let us heed that warning in time and return to him with humility, instead of hardening our hearts.
exp.2:5:
God says he destroyed nations. Their castles (towers and fortresses) lay in ruins, their streets were left empty, and their cities were left without people. Here "cut off" means to cut down or eliminate, and "destroyed" means leveled to the ground. The word for the people who lived in a place is simply the one who dwells there, which the verse above calls "inhabitant."

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. The words before this accuse Jerusalem of having corrupt leaders. God reminds them that other nations had already suffered his judgment, in the hope that Jerusalem would learn. But, according to the verses that follow, they did not listen and kept growing more corrupt. Scholars debate exactly which nations are meant.

God does not use the punishment of others to frighten us, but so that we may learn. Today we can look at the mistakes of others, and also our own, and correct our course in time, before our hearts grow hard.
exp.2:7:
God says to wait for the day when He will rise up to take the prey, that is, to act in justice against evil, like someone who takes what is rightfully theirs. His determination is to gather the nations and kingdoms so that He may pour out His anger on them. Zeal means His burning and exclusive love for what is just and holy. Consumed means destroyed, or purified, by that fire.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Earlier, God had punished other nations so that His people would learn and be corrected, but they rose early to corrupt their deeds. What follows shows the purpose: God will purify the lips of the peoples so that they call on Him and serve Him together. Some interpret the fire as the final judgment, others as a historical purification.

For today: do not take God's corrections lightly. If He shows you something crooked in your life, respond quickly with repentance, trusting that His goal is to heal and restore.
exp.2:10:
It says that in the coming day of restoration, God's people will no longer live in shame over their past rebellions. God will remove those who delight in pride, and his people will no longer be haughty on the holy mountain, which is Jerusalem. The word "haughty" in this verse means full of pride.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Earlier he warned of judgment for idolatry and injustice. Here he promises to purify the nations and his people. The words about not being ashamed can be understood as forgiveness and restoration; some also see them as a time when shame no longer dominates the people.

For today: if you have trusted in God, he can forgive you and heal your story. Ask him to remove the pride from your heart and teach you to live with humility and gratitude.
exp.2:12:
This verse promises that the small faithful group God keeps among his people will live with integrity: they will do no wrong and tell no lies, and their mouths will not speak to deceive. Being fed and cared for is like sheep looked after by their shepherd. Resting in peace describes lying down calmly, with no one to frighten them.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Earlier he has announced judgment on Jerusalem for its pride and rebellion. Now he promises to cleanse his people and leave a humble remnant that trusts in the name of the LORD. The verses that follow call for singing, because God himself is the King who dwells among them.

For today: the truthfulness of what we say grows out of trusting God. When we rest in his care, we have less need to lie or pretend. This week, try to speak honestly, even when it is hard, and hand your fears over to God.
exp.2:14:
It says that God has taken away the punishments that weighed on his people and has driven out their enemies. Now the Lord himself reigns in the midst of Israel, and for that reason they will no longer have to fear any harm.

The prophet Zephaniah is speaking. Before this passage he announced severe judgment for the sin of Judah. Now he describes a future restoration, when a faithful remnant will be cleansed and cared for by God. For that reason he invites Jerusalem to sing. Scholars debate whether the fulfillment was partial after the exile or points to God's final reign; many Christians see a reference to Christ here.

For today: when guilt or fear weighs on you, remember that God knows how to forgive and to stay close. Take a moment today to thank him in prayer, and bring him one specific worry, trusting that he is with you.
exp.1:13:
Zephaniah says that Nineveh will be left empty and in ruins. Herds will lie down there, and wild creatures of every kind. The creatures named in the verse are hard to identify with certainty; translators have suggested different birds and animals, so the exact species is uncertain. Their calls will be heard coming from the empty windows, there will be desolation on the threshold, and the fine cedar beams will be left exposed to view.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Assyria, with its capital Nineveh, considered itself unbeatable and had oppressed other peoples. God announces that no empire, however powerful it seems, lasts forever. The next verse shows the reason: its pride in saying, "I am, and there is none else beside me."

For today: do not place your security in your success, your possessions, or your strength. All of that can disappear. Live with humility and trust in God, who alone endures.
exp.0:8:
God says that on the day of his judgment he will punish those who "leap over the threshold." "To visit" means to come to judge and punish. "Fill" is the meaning of the word here. These are people who fill their masters' houses with stolen goods and with deceit.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, before the fall of Jerusalem. He warns that the day of the Lord is near and will reach both leaders and ordinary people. Some think that "leaping over the threshold" points to a pagan ritual, and others to forcing one's way in to steal. The text allows both readings. In any case, the sin is violence and fraud.

Examine how you earn your money and how you do your work. If you serve a boss, do not do it with lies or trickery. God sees what is hidden and desires honesty in everything.
exp.2:15:
On that day, the verse says, Jerusalem will be told, "Do not be afraid." Zion will be told, "Do not let your hands fall limp," meaning do not give up or lose your strength.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks on behalf of God. Earlier he announced judgment on the people, but here he ends with hope. God has taken away the punishment, driven out the enemies, and is present among his people. So the encouragement given does not come from circumstances, but from the presence of God. Scholars debate when this is fully fulfilled: some think of the return from exile, others of the final future.

When fear or weariness drains your strength, remember that God is with you. Tell him in prayer what you feel and rest in his presence, not only in your own strength.
exp.2:9:
From beyond the rivers of Cush, that is, from very distant lands, people who worship God will come. They are "My worshipers," those who honor and seek him, and "My scattered people," those who have been spread far apart. They will bring him an offering.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. First he announces judgment on the nations, and then he promises to purify the lips of the peoples so that all of them will serve him together. Scholars debate whether the "scattered people" are Jews living far from home or people from other nations who turn to God; both readings are possible. In either case, God promises to gather those who are far away.

For today: God reaches those who feel far away or scattered. Pray for people who are distant from God, and offer him your sincere worship without feeling too far away for him to receive it.
exp.1:10:
The LORD will be terrifying to Moab and Ammon when he starves all the gods of the earth. Then the nations of every shore will bow down in worship to him, each in its own place. The phrase "the nations of every shore" refers to distant lands, to peoples who live beyond the sea.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks on God's behalf, before the fall of Jerusalem. Moab and Ammon mocked God's people and grew proud. The Lord announces judgment on them and on other nations, but he also shows that his ultimate aim is for everyone to acknowledge him. Some scholars see here a hope for the nations; others, a submission through judgment.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your life, such as money, success, or pride. None of them can sustain you. Give your trust today to God alone.
exp.0:11:
God himself says that he will search Jerusalem with lamps, meaning with great care, so that nothing stays hidden. He will punish those who are "settled on their lees," a picture of wine left to rest without being stirred: people who are comfortable, stuck in place, and content in their complacency. They say to themselves that the LORD will do nothing, neither good nor bad. They think he neither rewards nor punishes, and that he does not care what they do.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, before the fall of Jerusalem. The people had fallen into idolatry and into a life of comfort without fear of God. The verses before and after speak of a coming day of judgment, in which the riches and the houses of those who trusted in themselves will be lost.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we live as if God does not see and does not matter. Let us pause, ask him to examine our hearts, and return to him with humility before we settle into indifference.
exp.0:4:
He says that God will also punish those who bow down on the rooftops to worship the host of heaven, the sun, the moon, and the stars. He also points to those who bow down and swear by the LORD, yet at the same time swear by Milcom. Their own words show a divided loyalty.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, announcing judgment on Judah and Jerusalem. The people were mixing the worship of the true God with the worship of other gods and the heavenly bodies. God did not accept a divided faith, and so he warns that the day of the Lord is coming.

For today: examine whether you give God first place or whether you share your trust with other things, such as money, success, or the opinions of others. Ask him to help you follow him with a whole heart.
exp.1:6:
The explanation says that the coast where the Philistines lived will belong to the small faithful group left from Judah. There they will find pasture for their flocks, and in the evening they will lie down among the houses of Ashkelon, a Philistine city. "Pasture" means they will tend their sheep there. "Attend to them" here means that God will care for them and help them. "Restore their captives" can be understood as bringing them back from exile or restoring their well-being; scholars read it in both ways.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Earlier he announced judgment on the Philistines, enemies of Judah. Now he promises care for the rest of his people, that is, those who remain faithful after the judgment.

For today: even when you see little strength or little hope, God does not forget those who trust in him. You can hand him your losses and wait for his care with patience.
exp.2:17:
God promises to gather those who grieve over the appointed feasts and who have carried the shame of being mocked. The reproach they bear is the disgrace of seeing their worship dishonored and their people looked down on. They are the faithful among Zion's people, weighed down by the scorn that fell on Jerusalem.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. After announcing judgment, he ends with hope: God will gather his people back, and he will do so with joy, like someone who delights over what belongs to him. The verse before it says that God rejoices over his people.

If you carry shame or years of weariness, God does not see you as a nuisance. He seeks you out, gathers you, and rejoices in you. Today you can bring him that burden in prayer, trusting that his time will come.
exp.1:1:
It says that people must gather together and reflect before it is too late. It speaks of a decree that takes effect, and of a day that passes quickly like chaff, the light husk of the grain that the wind carries away. "Burning anger" means a very strong wrath. The message is repeated three times: before the judgment of God comes, one must act.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks in the name of the LORD to the people of Judah, who had turned away from God. He warns them of a judgment that is near, yet he still opens a door for them to return. Scholars debate exactly which moment he has in mind, but the call is clear: repent while there is still time.

For today: do not put off until tomorrow what God asks of you today. If there is something you need to put right with Him or with others, do it now, with humility and sincerity.
exp.2:8:
In the future, God says, he will restore pure lips to the peoples. He means that he will cleanse the way they speak and the way they worship. The result is that all of them will call upon the name of the LORD and serve him shoulder to shoulder, united in heart and purpose.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Before this, he announced judgment, because the people would not turn from their wrongdoing and kept corrupting their actions. But judgment is not the final word: God cleanses in order to restore. Many believe this points to the salvation of people from all nations; some connect it to the end of the age, and others see a partial fulfillment before then.

For today: ask God to cleanse your words. Before you speak, ask yourself whether what you say honors God and builds unity. A tongue healed by him can become an instrument of worship and peace.
exp.1:11:
Zephaniah 2:12 says that the Cushites, the people of the land south of Egypt that the Bible calls Cush, will also be struck down by God's sword. "You too" means they will receive judgment, just as others will. The sword is an image of God's punishment.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Earlier he announced judgment on Philistia, Moab and Ammon. Now the judgment reaches the distant south, and then the north, to Assyria. By this he shows that his justice reaches all nations, not just one. Interpreters do not agree on why Cush is mentioned in particular. Some think it was a power of the time; others, that it stands for the far southern edge of the known world.

For today: God is just with everyone, and no one is beyond his reach. This invites us to live with humility, to let go of pride and to trust that he will do justice in his time.
exp.2:13:
This verse is an invitation to sing and celebrate. It is addressed to "Daughter of Zion," "Israel," and "Daughter of Jerusalem," which are poetic ways of speaking of God's people. The call to sing for joy and shout aloud means to cry out with gladness, and the call to be glad and rejoice with all your heart asks for a joy that is complete, without holding anything back.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks in the name of God. Earlier he announced judgment, but here he promises a future of restoration for a humble remnant that trusts in the name of the Lord. The reason for the joy appears in the verses that follow: God has taken away the punishment, has turned away the enemies, and reigns in the midst of his people.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed, pause and give thanks out loud for one specific thing God has done. Singing or giving thanks reminds us that God is near and that our hope does not depend only on circumstances.
exp.1:0:
The passage calls the people to come together and think seriously. Gather yourselves, gather together, and think carefully about your condition. The phrase that the verse renders as "shameful nation" is hard to translate: some versions say "shameless nation" or "without desire," and others say "a nation that is not wanted." For that reason it is understood in several ways, but in every case it is a call to a people who had turned away from God.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks, sent by God to Judah before a judgment that was announced. The verses that follow say that time is short: the day of the anger of the LORD is near. Even so, God invites them to seek Him with humility and righteousness, for there is hope of being protected.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to make you stop. Set aside a moment this week to examine your life before God, recognize what you need to correct, and return to Him with humility.
exp.0:10:
Wail, you who live in the Hollow, because all your merchants will be silenced, and everyone who weighs out silver will be cut off. To wail means to cry out in deep grief. To be cut off means to be completely destroyed. Many believe the Hollow refers to the lower part of Jerusalem, where the market was, though this cannot be known with certainty.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Judah had become filled with injustice, deceit, and indifference toward God. The merchants, who grew rich through fraud, would be reached by the judgment announced for that day, the day of the Lord.

For today: money and success do not protect us from God. We can examine how we work and do business, and ask ourselves whether we are honest and fair. Trusting in God, and not in our gains, gives us a more secure peace.
exp.1:9:
This is the punishment of Moab and Ammon because of their pride. "Pride" means believing oneself superior to others. Their taunting and mocking of the people of the LORD is what the verse names, meaning they insulted and humiliated them. Setting themselves above others, with arrogance, against the people of God is the heart of their offense.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, in a time of judgment on the nations. Moab and Ammon, neighbors of Israel, mocked the people of God and boasted of their power, even over their land. God says that he heard it all. His judgment shows that he defends his own people and does not overlook injustice or pride.

For today: when someone offends us, we can trust that God sees and knows how to do justice. It is also wise to examine our hearts, so that our strength or success does not lead us to despise others. Humility keeps us close to God.
exp.2:0:
This verse opens with "Woe!", a cry of grief and warning. It speaks of a city that is rebellious and defiled, that is, stained by sin, and also of oppressors, because it mistreats others. It is a serious accusation against a city that was meant to be holy.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Zephaniah, during the time of the kingdom of Judah. Many understand the city to be Jerusalem, although the text here does not name it. The following verses explain the reason: it did not listen to God, did not accept correction, did not trust in Him, and its leaders abused the people.

For today: when God corrects us, it is not wise to harden our hearts. We can ask ourselves whether we are listening to his voice, accepting counsel, and treating with justice and respect the people who are under our influence.
exp.0:1:
God says he will completely sweep away everything from the face of the earth. "I will completely sweep away" is a very strong expression: it means to remove everything entirely. "The face of the earth" means the surface of the earth. It is language of very serious judgment.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, during the reign of Josiah in Judah. The verses that follow show that the judgment would fall especially on Judah and Jerusalem because of their idolatry, such as the worship of Baal. Some understand these words as solemn, exaggerated language meant to warn of the judgment that was coming; others also see a reference to the final judgment. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but his warnings are also an invitation to return to him. Today you can ask yourself humbly: what have I put in place of God? Hand it over to him and trust in his mercy.
exp.1:4:
He says that God himself announces a judgment against those who live along the seacoast, by the Mediterranean. "Cherethites" is another name for the people of that region, and many believe it is related to the Cretans or to the Philistine peoples. This is not known with complete certainty. "Woe" expresses grief and warning. The "land of the Philistines" refers to the Philistines. God says that he will destroy them until no one is left.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, in the time of the kingdom of Judah. The Philistine cities were neighbors and often enemies of God's people. The message shows that God judges all nations. But the verse before invites the humble to seek him, and what follows promises that the remnant of Judah will be restored.

For today: let us not assume that God's judgment is only for others. Let us seek the Lord with humility and meekness, trusting that he cares for his own.
exp.0:17:
Money will not be able to save anyone when the day of God's judgment comes. "Jealousy" here means God's strong love, which does not tolerate evil. A "sudden end" means a quick and complete end. The verse uses forceful language to show that judgment will reach everyone who lives in rebellion against him.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks for God to Judah, probably in the days of King Josiah. The people had turned to idol worship and injustice, and they trusted in their security and their wealth. Scholars debate whether "the whole earth" refers to the entire world or to the land of Judah, and some see a fulfillment in more than one stage.

For today: examine where you place your trust. Money helps in life, but it cannot give you peace with God. Seek his forgiveness and live with humility and honesty.
exp.1:7:
God says that he has heard the mocking and insults of Moab and the Ammonites against his people. The words "reproach" and "insults" refer to offenses and hurtful words. "Taunted" means that they mocked Israel and made them feel small. "Threatened their borders" means that they boasted and acted aggressively toward their neighboring land, or that they moved against their territory; both readings are possible.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, in the days of Judah, before the fall of Jerusalem. Moab and Ammon were neighboring peoples, descendants of Lot. God announces judgment on the nations and comfort for the faithful remnant of Judah. For this reason the next verse promises justice: God does not overlook arrogance or the mistreatment of his people.

For today: if someone mocks you or mistreats you because of your faith, God sees and hears it. You can rest in the knowledge that he will act justly, and so avoid revenge and pray in peace.
exp.2:16:
This verse says that God is among his people, and that he is mighty to save. He rejoices over you with gladness and delights in you with singing. The phrase "he will quiet you with his love" can be understood to mean that his love is so deep that it brings you peace, leaving you at rest in his care.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks on behalf of God. After announcing judgment, he ends with a promise of restoration for Jerusalem. God removes the punishment, defeats the enemies, and tells his people not to be afraid. It points to a future time of salvation.

For today: when you feel unworthy or afraid, remember that God is not a distant judge. He draws near to you with joy and love. Today you can pray calmly, without pretending to be anything, trusting that he delights in you.
exp.1:3:
It says that four Philistine cities, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod and Ekron, will be destroyed. "Abandoned" means left empty, "left in ruins" means reduced to wreckage, and "uprooted" means pulled up from the ground. "Driven out at noon" suggests an attack in full daylight, without waiting for night.

There is a wordplay in Hebrew between the names of the cities and their fate, though that is best appreciated in the original language.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks in the name of the LORD. Earlier he had called Judah to seek God. Now he announces that judgment will reach the neighboring nations as well. The Philistines were peoples who opposed Israel. Scholars debate which exact historical events he has in mind.

For today: God rules over all the nations, and none is exempt from being accountable to him. This invites us to seek him with humility today, without trusting in our own strength or our own security.
exp.0:3:
God says he will stretch out his hand against Judah and against all who live in Jerusalem. It is a picture of judgment. He will also cut off from that place every remnant of Baal, a false god associated with fertility and rain. The verse names the idolatrous and pagan priests together, including those who served the LORD but mixed their faith with idolatry.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, in the days of King Josiah. The people said they followed God, but they also worshiped other gods. God does not judge on a whim, but because his people divided their hearts. The next verse confirms this.

Today we can ask ourselves what things compete with God in our hearts: money, fame, fear, or customs. God does not want only a faith of words, but a whole heart that seeks him sincerely.
exp.2:3:
Zephaniah 3:4 says that the prophets of Jerusalem were reckless, faithless men, meaning careless, without weight or seriousness, and untrustworthy, people who broke their word and neglected their duty. The priests profaned the sanctuary by treating what is holy as ordinary, and they did violence to the law by bending its teaching to suit themselves.

Zephaniah speaks in God's name, probably shortly before the reign of Josiah, although the date is not entirely certain. He is denouncing the leaders of Jerusalem: princes, judges, prophets, and priests. All of them had the responsibility to guide the people, but they failed. That is why the next verse contrasts their conduct with that of the LORD, who is righteous and does no iniquity.

Today it reminds us that whoever teaches the Word of God has a great responsibility. If we teach or guide others, we must be faithful to the truth, even when it is not popular. And if we listen, it is wise to compare what we hear with the Bible.
exp.2:19:
God promises that a time will come when he will gather and bring home his scattered people. "Fame" means a good reputation, and "praise" is a reason for honor. The BSB says God will "restore your captives," which means he will make his people return and be made whole again. He says he will do this before their very eyes, so they will see it with their own eyes.

God himself speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Earlier, he announced judgment on Judah for its sin. This closing section of the book ends on a note of hope: after correction, God promises to restore a humbled and scattered people. Scholars understand "that time" in different ways: the return from exile, a future fulfillment, or both.

For today: if you feel far away, ashamed, or broken, remember that God does not stop at punishment but seeks to restore. Trust his promise, even if you do not yet see the change, and return to him with hope.
exp.1:12:
God says he will stretch out his hand against the north, the direction from which the great northern empire lay. He will destroy Assyria and leave its capital, Nineveh, in complete ruin. The word "dry" describes land that is parched, without water. The great city will be left as dry as a desert.

Zephaniah, a prophet in the time of King Josiah, announces the message of the Lord. Earlier he spoke of judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon and Ethiopia. Now he comes to Assyria, a proud power that said in its heart, "I am, and there is no one else." The message shows that God rules over all nations and does not leave pride unanswered.

For today: do not put your trust in your strength, your success or your security, because all of that can vanish. Live with humility before God and trust in him, who sustains what truly endures.
exp.0:13:
It says that the great Day of the LORD, the day when God will act to judge, is near and coming quickly. Its approach is loud and urgent, and even the strong will be overcome with bitter cries. The verse makes the point that the coming of that day is fast and unavoidable.

Zephaniah was a prophet who spoke in Judah, probably in the time of King Josiah. God warns Jerusalem because its people had become indifferent. Some thought that God "will neither do good nor do evil," meaning that He is not involved in anything. For this reason He says He will search for them with lamps, like someone who examines every corner. Many see here a warning of judgment on Jerusalem and also a sign of the final judgment.

For today: do not live as if God were absent. Spend a few minutes this week examining your heart honestly before Him, and ask Him for help to correct what you have neglected.
exp.1:14:
This verse speaks of Nineveh, the great city of Assyria. It was carefree and lived in security, and in its heart it said: "I am it, and there is none besides me," meaning, "I am the only one; no one compares with me." But now it has become a ruin, a resting place for beasts. Those who pass by hiss and shake their fists, gestures of mockery or astonishment at its fall.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks, announcing God's judgment on the nations. Nineveh represented a proud and powerful empire. God warns that no nation, however strong it may seem, escapes his justice. According to history, Nineveh fell around 612 B.C.

For today: when success tempts us to think, "I don't need anyone, not even God," let us remember that everything we have is a gift. Let us cultivate humility and gratitude, trusting in God and not in our own strength.
exp.2:6:
God said that he hoped Jerusalem would revere him and accept his correction. Then its home would not be destroyed, despite all the punishment he had to bring. A home or city left in ruins is what the verse means by a dwelling being cut off. But the people rose early, meaning they eagerly hurried to corrupt everything they did.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. He has just recalled how he punished other nations, and he hoped his people would learn. Even so, they continued in their wickedness. This sets up the announcement of judgment and, afterward, of hope.

For today: when God corrects us through his Word, through wise counsel, or through consequences, let us not harden our hearts. Let us ask him for humility to change quickly, without delaying repentance.
exp.1:2:
God invites the humble of the earth, those who carry out his justice, to keep seeking him. He asks them to seek righteousness and humility. The words "perhaps you will be sheltered" mean that they may be protected on the day of the Lord's anger. The phrase "who carry out his justice" means that they live out what he requires.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks, delivering the message of the Lord to Judah before judgment. The verses before this one call the people to gather together and reflect while there is still time. Then the judgment reaches neighboring nations too, such as the Philistines. The word "perhaps" shows that protection depends on God's mercy, not on a right that we hold.

For today: do not wait for crises to come before you draw near to God. Seek his guidance in prayer today, act justly in your dealings, and respond with humility when you feel tempted to fight.
exp.2:1:
It says that the city did not heed God's voice when He spoke to her, and she accepted none of His correction. She does not trust in the LORD, and she has not drawn near to her God. Here "correction" means instruction and discipline, like that of a father who guides his child.

The prophet Zephaniah speaks, on God's behalf, to Jerusalem. Most readers understand "the city" to be Jerusalem, although the text does not name it here. The opening cry is a serious warning. The verses that follow show that her leaders, judges, prophets, and priests were abusing their position. The problem was not a lack of warning, but a closed heart.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I listen to God when He corrects me? This week, read a passage of the Bible with humility and ask Him to show you something you need to change. Then obey, even if it costs you.
exp.0:5:
This verse continues the list of people whom God will judge. It speaks of those who turn back from following the LORD, and of those who neither seek the LORD nor inquire of Him, meaning they never wanted to know his will or ask him for direction.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah, addressing Judah and Jerusalem. The people mixed the worship of the LORD with the worship of Baal and the stars. Here God points out another sin: indifference. They were not only doing wrong things; they had also stopped seeking him.

For today: it is not enough to avoid doing wrong; we also need to seek God every day. Set aside time to pray, read the Bible, and ask him what he wants from you, so that your faith does not grow cold little by little.
exp.0:14:
This verse describes the "day of the LORD" with a series of very strong images: wrath, distress, trouble, destruction, and desolation. "Trouble" means a situation with no way out. "Desolation" is total ruin. "Darkness," "gloom," and "clouds and blackness" speak of a dark sky, with no light and no hope.

Zephaniah speaks on behalf of God to the kingdom of Judah, probably in the days of King Josiah, though the text gives no further detail. The people had fallen into idolatry and injustice. The prophet announces that God is going to judge sin, and the preceding verses show that no one will be able to escape by trusting in their riches.

For today: let us not take God's holiness lightly. His judgment is real, but it also invites us to turn back to Him with humility while there is still time. Today you can examine your heart and ask Him to forgive what you need to correct.
exp.2:18:
When that time comes, God says, he himself will deal with everyone who has oppressed his people. He promises to save those who are lame, to gather those who have been scattered, and to appoint praise and honor for those who were disgraced throughout the earth. The shame they suffered will be turned into a good name and a public reputation.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. He first announced judgment, but the book ends with hope for a battered and scattered people. Interpreters see it as a promise for the return from exile, and many Christians also see it fulfilled in part in Christ and fully in the future.

Today we can come to God with our wounds and failures without hiding them. He does not despise the weak or the one who has gone astray; he seeks them out, sustains them, and can restore their dignity.
exp.2:11:
God promises that, after cleansing his people of pride, he will leave in Jerusalem a humble group of people. Those who are meek and humble are people who do not trust in their own power, their money, or their pride, but who lean on God. They will trust in the name of the LORD, which means they will rely on who God is and on his faithful character.

God speaks through the prophet Zephaniah. Earlier, he announces judgment on Jerusalem for its rebellion and its pride. Here, however, he promises restoration. The verses that follow show that this remnant will live with honesty and in peace, and so it will be able to sing with joy.

For today: God draws near to those who recognize their need. Today you can stop pretending to be strong and tell him sincerely: "Lord, I trust in you." That humble trust gives you a peace that pride never gives.

sum.1: Zephaniah calls the people to seek the LORD, with humility and righteousness, before the day of his anger arrives. He announces judgment on the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Ethiopia, and Nineveh because of their pride and wickedness, while the rest of Judah will be cared for and restored. Nineveh, which felt secure, will be left a desolate ruin.
sum.2: Zephaniah rebukes Jerusalem because its leaders are corrupt and did not listen to God, and he announces that God will judge the nations. But afterward he promises to cleanse and humble his people, to leave behind a faithful remnant, and to gather the scattered. God will save them, and he will rejoice over them with singing.
sum.0: God speaks to Zephaniah during the time of King Josiah, and he announces a harsh judgment on Judah and Jerusalem because of their idolatry, their injustice, and their indifference toward him. The "day of the LORD" is coming, a day of wrath and distress, when neither money nor fortified cities will be able to save anyone.
